chapter: Union, publishers, race and Harlem nightlife
title: Bill Robinson's money to a cop and Otis Johnson's gold pistol
summary: Anecdotes of Bojangles paying a cop and trumpeter Otis Johnson fighting a kid over an autograph in Hartford.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: I'll tell you an incident but don't put it on tape.

...... Not only that, our soloist and our set was the first Negro band to open at the Strand Theatre downtown... During the intermission, you know you walk out in a little fresh air, there was a cop on the corner. Bill Robinson walked up, put his hand in his pocket, and gave this cop money, if I'm lyin'. I hope I'll never play a note. The cop said, "What is this for?" He said, "My name is Bojangles."
Just like that? He gave the money away?
And then Otis Johnson, you know, the trumpet player - boy, Otis was a killer. He can't gamble, if he play cards if he lose, he want to fight. Another time you came to Connecticut -
Hartford, Connecticut. That's what I tried to tell them but you shut me up. Midge Williams?

So he wanted his autograph. Sunday morning I think it was. So he always carried this pistol, a gold pistol. So a kid, he just asked, can I have your autograph please. He took out his pistol and started fighting. He shot up in the air and he whipped that kid over the automobile that was parked outside...
